knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", echo = FALSE)

This notebook is the record of the project: how the method and the
simulated test data were developed, and every check run on them. Results are
written down as observed at the time and are **not** recomputed when the
page is rebuilt. Later findings are added as new dated entries (or dated
notes) rather than by editing earlier results.

Where an entry has a reproducing script, it is in `dev/checks/`. Run scripts
from the package root; outputs go to `$SURVIVER_CHECKS_OUT` (default: a
temporary folder).

## Status and open questions

*Last updated 2026-11-25.*

| Question | Status | Entry |
|---|---|---|
| Does `fit_ve()` recover a known VE(t)? | Yes, broadly; 92–93% of days inside the 90% CrI | [7](#e07) |
| Why is the estimated curve about a week behind the truth? | Reporting time vs infection time. **Deferred** to the planned delay extension | [7](#e07) |
| Why is late (90+ day) VE underestimated in the waning scenario? | About half explained by calendar time leaking into time since vaccination. Remainder within noise | [8](#e08), [9](#e09) |
| Do unreported (immune) infections in the risk set bias VE? | No detectable effect | [8](#e08) |
| Does the FoI offset improve precision? | Not in this simulation once calendar time is adjusted for | [9](#e09) |
| Is the remaining late bias real or chance? | **Open**: needs replicate simulations | — |
| Is a frailty term needed? | **Open**: decide after replicate simulations | — |
| What value of `theta` (infectiousness of vaccinated cases) should the case-study analysis use? | **Open**: the workshop text said 0.5, its code used 1, the package default is 0 | [1](#e01), [6](#e06) |
| Should the HERMES reporting-seed bug be reported upstream? | **Open**: affects reproducibility of all HERMES case-study data | [4](#e04) |

### Next steps

1. Let transmission vary over calendar time in the Stan model (e.g. a random
   walk on `log_beta` by day or week), keeping the FoI offset.
2. Run 20–50 replicate HERMES simulations per scenario to measure bias and
   interval coverage, rather than judging from one realisation.
3. Revisit frailty once (1) and (2) are done.
4. Extend the method to account for the delay between infection and
   reporting.

## 1. 2026-06-16 to 19 — Method developed at the Lorentz Center workshop {#e01}

**Context.** Group D (Fanny Bergström, David Price, Nathalie Dean, Hein
Putter, Kylie Ainslie) at the Lorentz Center workshop *Connecting Survival
Analysis and Infectious Disease Modelling* (Leiden, 15–19 June 2026). Aim:
improve the efficiency of VE estimation by using the force of infection
experienced by different subpopulations.

**Data.** The workshop case study: a HERMES simulation of 200,000 people
generated by the organisers, provided as `demographic_data.rds`,
`vaccination_data.rds` and `incidence_data_reduced.rds`. The VE generating
that data is not known to participants.

**Method developed** (workshop repo, branch `group-D`, `analysis/group-D/`):

- `data_wrangling.R`: merge the data, sample a cohort of 10,000, daily
  incidence by age group and vaccination status, counting-process data split
  at vaccination, expansion to person-days, prevalence from reported cases
  (7-day infectious period starting 2 days before reporting).
- `prepare_stan_data.R`: age-structured FoI
  \(\bar I(t_c, a) = \sum_{a'} C_{a'a} I^{\text{eff}}_{a'}(t_c - 1) / N_a\)
  using the POLYMOD Netherlands contact matrix, plus an overall-prevalence
  version; person-days aggregated to cells.
- `model.stan`: Poisson approximation to a Cox model,
  \(\log\mu = \log\beta + \log\bar I + \log D + \gamma(t)V\), with a daily
  random walk on \(\gamma(t)\) and \(\gamma(1) \sim N(-1, 1)\).
- `run_model.R`: fits the age-structured and overall-prevalence versions.
- `analysis_Poisson_and_Cox.R` (Hein Putter, 2026-06-19): frequentist
  Poisson and Cox fits with piecewise-constant hazard ratios.

**Check: parameter recovery with simulated outcomes** (`simulate_validate.R`,
2026-06-17). Event counts were simulated from the model itself under a known
\(\log\beta = -4.4\) and a rise-then-wane \(\gamma(t)\), keeping the real
covariate structure, then refitted.

```{r, fig.alt = "Workshop parameter-recovery check: posterior median and 90% interval of gamma(t) against the true simulated curve; recovery is good for about two weeks, then the estimate flattens."}
fig("2026-06-17_workshop_recovery.png")
```

Results recorded in the workshop vignette:

- \(\log\beta\) recovered accurately (true −4.4, posterior median −4.40).
- \(\gamma(t)\) recovered well for about two weeks, then flattened with
  rapidly widening uncertainty. This followed event sparsity in the
  vaccinated group (events near zero by days 13–20), not a sampler failure.
  Earlier sampler problems were fixed by a non-centred parameterisation
  (`model_noncentered.stan`).
- On the case-study data, VE rose to about 88% by day 15, then appeared to
  plateau at 70–72% from day 45–90 (judged likely prior-driven), with an
  early dip to about −22% at days 2–3 (plausibly a reporting-delay effect).

**Notes added 2026-11-25.**

- The vignette states \(\theta = 0.5\) (vaccinated cases half as infectious),
  but `prepare_stan_data.R` used `theta <- 1` (vaccinated cases not
  infectious at all).
- The scripts hard-coded the study end (93 days in one place, 90 in another);
  see [entry 6](#e06).
- The case-study VE is unknown, so these checks could only test the model
  against itself, not against a known truth. This motivated entry 2.

## 2. 2026-09-10 — HERMES extended with waning VE; first ground-truth datasets {#e02}

**Why.** To validate the method against data where the true VE(t) is known,
HERMES needed vaccine protection that changes with time since vaccination,
and a scenario designed so that waning could in principle be detected.

**Changes to HERMES** (fork `kylieainslie/ibm_hermes`; these changes were
left uncommitted until 2026-11-25, commit `24fc257` on branch
`waning-vaccine-effectiveness`):

- `compute_time_varying_ve()` in `lib/ibm_core.R`: VE rises linearly from 0
  to a peak over `ve_ramp_days`, then decays exponentially with half-life
  `ve_half_life` towards `ve_floor`. Applied to susceptibility only, in both
  `run_ibm()` and `rerun_ibm()`.
- New defaults in `lib/ibm_parameters.R`, with their basis:

| Parameter | Value | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| `vaccine_effectiveness` (peak) | 0.8 | High end of measured influenza VE; optimistic, which makes waning easier to see (Ferdinands et al. 2018) |
| `ve_ramp_days` | 14 | About two weeks for protective antibodies; VE studies start the "fully vaccinated" window at day 15 |
| `ve_half_life` | 45 days | Exponential fit to Ferdinands et al.'s A(H3N2) estimates gives about 46 days; consistent with Chung et al. 2024 |
| `ve_floor` | 0.1 | Assumption; little data beyond 180 days |

- Recalibrated, to be closer to seasonal influenza: `prob_hospital` from 0.3
  to 0.0015 (calibrated by simulation to about 1.5% of symptomatic cases
  hospitalised), and `disease_mortality_rate` from 0.01–0.7 to
  0.00003–0.003 per day (verified by simulation at about 0.06% IFR under 60
  and 0.5% over 60).
- A check of other HERMES parameters against influenza literature found the
  mean incubation period (about 5 days) is 2.5–3 times longer than published
  estimates. Left unchanged.
- **Side effect:** these are package-wide defaults, so every HERMES scenario
  now has waning VE and lower hospitalisation and mortality unless the
  script overrides them.

**Scenario design** (`lib/ibm_waning_scenario.R`): 10 initial infections and
20 days without vaccination, then 16 rounds of 10 days, each vaccinating 3%
of the remaining eligible population (seed `rng_seed + round`).

**Choice of `transmission_prob`.** The default (0.1) gives an epidemic that
is over before most people are vaccinated. A sweep without vaccination
(10,000 people, 180 days):

| `transmission_prob` | Peak infectious | Peak day | Extinct by | Final attack rate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.035 | 1,603 | 41 | day 126 | 71.1% |
| **0.02** | 335 | 88 | not by day 180 | 32.4% |
| 0.015 | 46 | 63 | not by day 180 | 5.0% |
| 0.012 | 15 | 4 | day 73 | 0.3% |
| 0.01 | 14 | 6 | day 102 | 0.6% |

With 0.035, vaccinated cases bunched in the first 45 days after vaccination
(79/63/60/38/12/9/2 cases in the 0–7/7–14/14–30/30–45/45–60/60–90/90+ day
ranges). With 0.02 they spread across the full range (28/19/25/18/19/40/44),
which is what's needed to see waning. 0.02 was chosen.

**Output.** Two scenarios, `waning` (`ve_floor = 0.1`) and `no_waning`
(`ve_floor = 0.8`), each 10,000 people, committed to the workshop repo as
`data/ve_test_scenarios/` (commit `9f0d72d`). The commit message reports a
piecewise-Poisson check, run outside any repository, that recovered the true
curve well in both. That check is not recorded anywhere and is superseded by
[entry 7](#e07).

**Notes added 2026-11-25.**

- The committed script and the HERMES vignette described a population of
  100,000 and output paths that did not match the data. The data were in fact
  generated with 10,000 people (confirmed from the saved parameters).
- The reported-case files cannot be reproduced; see [entry 4](#e04).

## 3. 2026-11-25 — Work consolidated into the surviver package {#e03}

The work was spread across branches of two repositories (workshop `group-D`
and HERMES), plus uncommitted changes. It was reorganised as:

| What | Where |
|---|---|
| Estimation code, datasets, vignettes, this notebook | `surviver` R package (this repository), MIT licence |
| HERMES waning-VE code | `kylieainslie/ibm_hermes`, branch `waning-vaccine-effectiveness` |
| Workshop record (original scripts, vignettes) | `kylieainslie/lorentz_center_workshop`, branch `group-D`, left in place |

The package's data scripts load HERMES from a local clone (`HERMES_PATH`) and
record the HERMES commit in each dataset, so HERMES can keep changing without
a pull request upstream. The workshop case-study data (200,000 people) is not
included, as it belongs to the workshop organisers. Both Stan models are
kept: `ve_noncentered.stan` (default) and `ve_centered.stan`.

---

## 4. 2026-11-25 — HERMES scenario made reproducible; data regenerated {#e04}

**What was done** (HERMES commit `6c9ab73`). The scenario script was turned
into `simulate_waning_scenario(ve_floor, ...)`, whose defaults match the
September data, and `export_waning_scenario()`.

**Check: does it reproduce the committed data?** Both scenarios were rerun
and compared with `data/ve_test_scenarios/`:

- Population, vaccination data and saved parameters: **identical**.
- Reported cases: **different** (e.g. 1,588 vs 1,568 in the waning
  scenario), and different again on a second run (1,582).

**Cause.** `obtain_incidence_data()` calls `set.seed(delay_params$rng_seed)`,
but `get_default_delay_parameters()` has no `rng_seed`, so it calls
`set.seed(NULL)` and draws a fresh seed every run. Infections and
vaccinations are reproducible; which cases are reported, and when, is not.

**Fix.** The scenario function sets `delay_params$rng_seed <- params$rng_seed`.
Two runs are now identical. The September reported-case files cannot be
recovered, so the datasets were regenerated (`data-raw/ve_test_scenarios.R`)
and the package versions are now the reference. They differ from the
workshop copies only in the reported-case table.

**Implication.** The same unseeded step probably affects every HERMES
dataset, including the workshop case study. A one-line fix to
`get_default_delay_parameters()` would solve it upstream.

---

## 5. 2026-11-25 — The simulated datasets {#e05}

`ve_sim_waning` and `ve_sim_no_waning` are the reference test data for the
method. Generated by `data-raw/ve_test_scenarios.R` with HERMES commit
`6c9ab73`. Summaries below from `dev/checks/2026-11-25_00_simulated_data.R`.

**Design.** Both use the same synthetic population and settings; only
`ve_floor` differs.

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Population | 10,000 (0–4: 514; 5–17: 1,693; 18–49: 3,890; 50–64: 1,937; 65+: 1,966) |
| Transmission | Household, school, workplace and community contacts; `transmission_prob = 0.02`; 10 initial infections |
| Study length | 180 days |
| Vaccination | None for days 1–20; then 16 rounds of 10 days, each vaccinating 3% of the remaining eligible population |
| Natural history | 80% of infections symptomatic; infectious for a mean of 7 days |
| Reporting | Symptomatic cases reported after a delay (Poisson, mean 2 days, maximum 6); 10% of symptomatic cases never reported |
| VE | Acts on susceptibility only. Ramps from 0 to 0.8 over 14 days; then decays with half-life 45 days towards 0.1 (`waning`) or stays at 0.8 (`no_waning`) |
| Random seed | 2026 (rounds use 2026 + round; reporting uses 2026) |

```{r, fig.alt = "True VE by days since vaccination: both rise linearly to 0.8 at day 14; the waning curve then decays towards 0.1 while the no-waning curve stays at 0.8."}
fig("2026-11-25_00_true_ve.png")
```

**Contents.**

| | Waning | No waning |
|---|---|---|
| Vaccinated | 3,842 (38.4%) | 3,846 (38.5%) |
| Reported cases | 1,566 (1,558 by day 180) | 1,559 |
| Ever infected by day 180 (incl. unreported) | 2,185 | 2,182 |
| Vaccinated people reported on or before their vaccination date | 326 | 372 |
| Peak week of reported cases | from day 63 (117 cases) | from day 77 (163 cases) |

```{r, fig.alt = "Weekly reported cases and cumulative vaccination coverage for each scenario; the no-waning epidemic peaks more sharply and ends earlier, while the waning epidemic continues at a lower level to day 180."}
fig("2026-11-25_00_epidemic.png")
```

Cases among vaccinated people, reported after vaccination and by day 180, by
days since vaccination (the information available to estimate VE(t)):

| Days since vaccination | 0–6 | 7–13 | 14–29 | 30–44 | 45–59 | 60–89 | 90+ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Waning | 23 | 24 | 21 | 15 | 22 | 36 | 41 |
| No waning | 27 | 24 | 25 | 14 | 14 | 11 | 3 |

**Things to be aware of.**

- The two runs are **not** paired realisations of one epidemic: their
  epidemic curves differ from the first weeks, before VE could matter.
- HERMES vaccinates people who have already been infected, hence the
  326/372 vaccinated people reported before vaccination.
- About 28% of infections are never reported (asymptomatic or missed). They
  are immune but look susceptible in the data.
- Reports can fall after day 180 (up to day 190 in the waning scenario).
- `general_mortality_rate = NULL` switches on HERMES's background mortality,
  separate from disease deaths. Deaths are not in the exported data.
- The scenarios are stylised, not a realistic influenza season (see the
  incubation-period note in [entry 2](#e02)).

## 6. 2026-11-25 — Analysis code ported into the package {#e06}

The workshop scripts were rewritten as package functions (`ve_population()`,
`daily_incidence()`, `daily_prevalence()`, `counting_process()`,
`expand_person_days()`, `force_of_infection()`, `make_stan_data()`,
`fit_ve()`, `extract_ve()`, `plot_ve()`, `true_ve()`, `simulate_counts()`),
with unit tests. Behaviour that differs from the workshop scripts:

| Change | Workshop scripts | Package | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Study end | Hard-coded 93 and 90 days | Taken from the data; cases reported later are censored | The simulated data run to 180 days and would have been silently cut |
| Infectious period | 8 days when `duration_infection = 7` | 7 days | Off-by-one in the original sequence |
| `theta` default | 1 (vaccinated cases not infectious) | 0 (as infectious as unvaccinated) | Matches HERMES, where VE acts on susceptibility only. The case-study value is still to be decided |
| Column naming | Columns renamed by position | Renamed by name | Positional renames break silently |
| Never vaccinated | `vax_status` could be `NA` | 0 | — |
| Speed | Nested loops | Vectorised; person-days for 10,000 people in about 1 s | — |

The POLYMOD matrix (`polymod_nl`) was checked to be identical to the
workshop's `contact_matrix_NL.rds`.

## 7. 2026-11-25 — Recovery of VE(t) on simulated data {#e07}

**Question.** Does `fit_ve()` (non-centred random-walk model, default
settings) recover the true VE(t) in the two HERMES scenarios, and can it tell
waning from no waning?

**Data.** `ve_sim_waning` and `ve_sim_no_waning` ([entry 5](#e05)).

**Method.** Full population, age-structured FoI from `polymod_nl` with
`theta = 0`, infectious period 7 days starting 2 days before reporting, lag 1
day. Every day since vaccination gets its own bin (160 bins). 4 chains,
1,000 warm-up + 1,000 sampling iterations, `adapt_delta = 0.95`, seed 42.

**Script.** `dev/checks/2026-11-25_01_recovery.R` (about 1–2 minutes).

**Results.**

- Converged in both scenarios: max R-hat 1.004, min bulk ESS about 3,900,
  1 divergent transition in 4,000 (waning) and none (no waning). 30–45 s per
  fit.
- `log_beta` −4.51 (waning), −4.48 (no waning). `sigma_gamma` 0.12 and 0.18.
- True VE inside the 90% CrI on 93% (waning) and 92% (no waning) of days.

Average VE over each range of days since vaccination (true VE is averaged over
the same days; e.g. 0.20 for days 1–6 is the mean of the ramp 0.06…0.34):

| Days since vaccination | Waning: true | Waning: estimate (90% CrI) | No waning: true | No waning: estimate (90% CrI) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1–6 | 0.20 | 0.22 (−0.12, 0.45) | 0.20 | 0.11 (−0.31, 0.40) |
| 7–13 | 0.57 | 0.32 (0.05, 0.51) | 0.57 | 0.27 (−0.06, 0.49) |
| 14–29 | 0.73 | 0.61 (0.45, 0.74) | 0.80 | 0.64 (0.45, 0.78) |
| 30–44 | 0.59 | 0.68 (0.54, 0.80) | 0.80 | 0.74 (0.58, 0.84) |
| 45–59 | 0.49 | 0.57 (0.38, 0.71) | 0.80 | 0.74 (0.58, 0.85) |
| 60–89 | 0.38 | 0.43 (0.16, 0.62) | 0.80 | 0.82 (0.67, 0.91) |
| 90+ | 0.23 | 0.01 (−0.70, 0.44) | 0.80 | 0.84 (0.47, 0.96) |

```{r, fig.alt = "Estimated VE by day since vaccination with 90% credible band, against the true curve, for the waning and no-waning scenarios."}
fig("2026-11-25_01_recovery.png")
```

**Observations.**

1. The two scenarios are clearly distinguished: a rise then decline in the
   waning scenario, a plateau near 0.8 in the no-waning scenario. Unlike the
   workshop check ([entry 1](#e01)), the curve is informed by data well
   beyond two weeks, because these scenarios were designed to have
   vaccinated cases at long times since vaccination.
2. The estimate lags the truth by about a week. Shifting the true curve
   right minimises the mean absolute error (days 1–120) at 6 days (waning)
   and 7–8 days (no waning). "Days since vaccination" is measured to the
   reporting day, while protection acts at infection, roughly 5 days
   (incubation) plus 2 days (reporting delay) earlier.
3. In the waning scenario the estimate falls below the truth after about
   day 90 (to around 0 against a true 0.2), with wide intervals that still
   contain the truth.

**Conclusion.** The method works on this data. The lag is expected and will
be handled by the planned extension for delays. The late underestimate needs
explaining (entries [8](#e08) and [9](#e09)).

---

## 8. 2026-11-25 — Do unreported infections in the risk set cause the late drop? {#e08}

**Question.** About 28% of HERMES infections are never reported (20%
asymptomatic, plus 10% of symptomatic cases missed). These people are immune
but stay "at risk" in the data, mostly in the unvaccinated group. Does this
explain the late underestimate in [entry 7](#e07)?

**Method.** Regenerate both scenarios with HERMES to recover every person's
true `time_of_infection` (the regenerated runs were checked to be identical
to the packaged data). Refit the entry 7 model twice per scenario:

- **reported only**: as in entry 7;
- **true risk set**: people infected but never reported are censored at their
  true infection time.

Events (reported cases at their report day), FoI and all settings are
unchanged, so any difference is due only to the unreported infections.

**Script.** `dev/checks/2026-11-25_02_true_risk_set.R` (needs a local
`ibm_hermes` clone; about 2–3 minutes).

**Results.**

- Unreported infections censored: 627 (waning; 570 unvaccinated and 57
  vaccinated at infection) and 623 (no waning; 596 and 27).
- Estimates are essentially unchanged:

| Days since vaccination | True VE | Reported only | True risk set |
|---|---|---|---|
| 14–29 | 0.73 | 0.61 | 0.61 |
| 30–44 | 0.59 | 0.68 | 0.68 |
| 60–89 | 0.38 | 0.43 | 0.43 |
| 90–119 | 0.28 | 0.13 | 0.14 |
| 120+ | 0.20 | −0.08 | −0.07 |

*(waning scenario; averages over each range of days)*

- Mean error from day 90 on (estimate − truth): −0.22 vs −0.21 (waning);
  +0.04 vs +0.05 (no waning). Coverage 92–93% in all four fits.

```{r, fig.alt = "Estimated VE with the reported-only and true risk sets overlaid; the two curves are nearly identical in both scenarios."}
fig("2026-11-25_02_true_risk_set.png")
```

**Conclusion.** Unreported infections are not the cause. Removing about 600
people (roughly 10% of the remaining unvaccinated, leaving gradually) barely
changes the unvaccinated person-time, and the overall level is absorbed by
`log_beta`. A correction for unreported infections is not a priority for
VE(t).

---

## 9. 2026-11-25 — Is calendar time leaking into time since vaccination? {#e09}

**Question.** Long times since vaccination are only observed late in the
epidemic (you must have been vaccinated early). The model has one
transmission level for the whole study and relies on the FoI offset to track
calendar time. If the FoI fits poorly late in the epidemic, the leftover
error lands on the late time-since-vaccination bins. Does adjusting for
calendar day remove the late drop?

**Method.** Frequentist Poisson GLMs on the same cells as the Stan model,
with one VE per range of days since vaccination (piecewise constant):

- **A**: one baseline + FoI offset (the Stan model's structure);
- **B**: a separate baseline for each calendar day + FoI offset;
- **C**: a separate baseline for each calendar day + age group, no FoI
  (equivalent to a Cox model on calendar time).

Days with no cases at all are dropped for B and C, since they carry no
information once each day has its own baseline. The true VE per range is the
mean over vaccinated person-days.

**Script.** `dev/checks/2026-11-25_03_calendar_time.R` (seconds; base R).

**Results** (waning scenario, VE with 90% CI):

| Days since vaccination | Cases (vaccinated) | True VE | A | B | C |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1–6 | 23 | 0.20 | 0.09 (−0.29, 0.35) | 0.08 (−0.30, 0.35) | 0.07 (−0.31, 0.35) |
| 7–13 | 24 | 0.57 | 0.18 (−0.15, 0.42) | 0.19 (−0.14, 0.42) | 0.18 (−0.15, 0.42) |
| 14–29 | 21 | 0.73 | 0.68 (0.55, 0.78) | 0.69 (0.55, 0.78) | 0.68 (0.55, 0.78) |
| 30–44 | 15 | 0.59 | 0.73 (0.58, 0.82) | 0.74 (0.60, 0.83) | 0.74 (0.60, 0.83) |
| 45–59 | 22 | 0.49 | 0.53 (0.32, 0.67) | 0.55 (0.36, 0.68) | 0.55 (0.36, 0.68) |
| 60–89 | 36 | 0.38 | 0.42 (0.24, 0.56) | 0.47 (0.30, 0.60) | 0.47 (0.30, 0.60) |
| 90–119 | 28 | 0.28 | 0.10 (−0.23, 0.35) | 0.21 (−0.09, 0.43) | 0.22 (−0.08, 0.44) |
| 120+ | 13 | 0.21 | −0.11 (−0.76, 0.30) | 0.05 (−0.53, 0.41) | 0.07 (−0.50, 0.43) |

Case-weighted mean error from day 90 on: **A −0.22, B −0.10, C −0.08**
(waning); A 0.00, B +0.03, C +0.04 (no waning, where there are only 3
vaccinated cases at 90–119 days and none at 120+, so 120+ is not estimable).

```{r, fig.alt = "Point estimates and 90% intervals by range of days since vaccination for models A, B and C, with the true VE marked; B and C sit closer to the truth than A from day 90 on."}
fig("2026-11-25_03_calendar_time.png")
```

**Observations.**

1. Model A reproduces the Stan model's late error (−0.22), so the
   piecewise GLM is a fair stand-in for this question.
2. A per-day baseline roughly halves the late error. Earlier ranges barely
   change.
3. The remaining error (about −0.1) is well inside the intervals (41
   vaccinated cases after day 90); one realisation cannot separate it from
   chance.
4. B and C give almost identical estimates and interval widths: once each day
   has its own baseline, the POLYMOD-based FoI adds nothing beyond an age
   effect here. This may reflect that POLYMOD contacts do not describe how
   HERMES transmits (households, schools, workplaces). Relevant to the
   project's premise that FoI improves precision; worth revisiting with a
   FoI built from the simulation's own contact structure.

**Conclusion.** Calendar-time confounding explains about half of the late
underestimate. Next: add calendar-time flexibility to the Stan model, then
judge any remaining bias, and the need for frailty, with replicate
simulations.
